parts.note: a rider who is up on a horse yet with neither leg thrown over its back sits with both legs on one flank

explanation.surface: A jockey is mounted but has not quite finished climbing across.
explanation.definitionFit: The old ladies' riding style keeps both legs on one flank of the horse, so the rider is up without straddling.

parts.note: a dense yellow fog was nicknamed after a thick pea-based dish

explanation.surface: A dense fog of this kind lies over the countryside away from the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: London's dense smogs were called pea-soupers, named after thick pea broth.
explanation.definitionFit: A thick broth gave its name to dense fog, called a pea-souper.

indicators.note: one piece eats the other, holding it inside

parts.note: DD, Doctor of Divinity, stands for a clergyman
an apple is a fruit

explanation.surface: A clergyman was seen munching some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' looks like 'seen' but means mottled, and 'divine' is a clergyman, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Mottled with patches of colour, as a horse's coat is marked with round spots.

parts.note: a spring is a source of water, a well
oiled and loaded are both slang for drunk

explanation.surface: Someone drunk is likened to a snare for catching animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Well-oiled looks like one word for drunk but splits into two pieces. A gin trap is an animal snare with sprung jaws, nothing to do with the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A gin trap's jaws are held open under tension from a coiled spring, set to snap shut.

parts.note: Dis is another name for Pluto, Roman god of the underworld
per se is Latin for by itself

explanation.surface: A broadcast transmitted from the distant planet Pluto with no help.
explanation.definitionFit: To broadcast seed is to scatter it widely, spreading it about.

clue.text: Hang about! Vitamin A is served up without a name!

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is removed
in a down clue served up means brought upwards, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: retinol is the chemical name of vitamin A
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A protest that a vitamin supplement arrived without any label on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' reverses RETINOL to LONITER; 'without a name' removes the N.
explanation.definitionFit: To linger idly or dawdle around a place, the verb in the imperative.

clue.text: Lies low, heading off for a few days in Rome

indicators.note: the head of the word, its opening letter, is taken off

parts.note: someone who lies low keeps out of sight, i.e. hides

explanation.surface: Someone keeps out of sight while setting off on a short Roman holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' removes the H from HIDES. The Roman calendar's Ides fell on the 13th or 15th of the month.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ides were fixed dates in the Roman calendar, mid-month days such as the Ides of March.

indicators.note: losing means a part is taken away

parts.note: to cogitate is to think hard, to deliberate
in music the rate, or tempo, is the time

explanation.surface: A composer thinks deeply and loses track of the hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' removes RATE from DELIBERATES. Léo Delibes wrote the ballet Coppélia.
explanation.definitionFit: Léo Delibes was a French Romantic composer of ballets and the opera Lakmé.

clue.text: But are these bank records prepared by tellers?

definitions.text: But are these bank records prepared by tellers?

parts.words: But are these bank records prepared by tellers?
parts.note: a bank's account summaries are named with a word meaning things told, and tellers are both bank clerks and those who tell

explanation.surface: A query about whether cashiers draw up customers' account summaries.
explanation.walkthrough: Tellers are bank cashiers but also people who tell; what they tell are spoken assertions, the same word as bank account summaries.
explanation.definitionFit: Bank account summaries share their name with spoken declarations, which tellers make.

clue.text: Office in which strikers may be dismissed

definitions.text: Office in which strikers may be dismissed

parts.words: Office in which strikers may be dismissed
parts.note: strikers here are batsmen at cricket, and the official on the field gives them out

explanation.surface: A workplace where staff who walk out on strike risk being sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: Strikers suggests industrial action; in cricket the batsman facing the bowling is the striker, and the umpire gives him out.
explanation.definitionFit: The post or role of a match official in cricket, who rules batsmen out, is that official's office.

clue.text: It strengthens the arm of a peaceful nation

indicators.note: of here means taken out of, so the answer is a run of letters drawn from the words that follow

explanation.surface: Defence aid that bolsters the armed forces of a nonviolent country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arm' suggests armed forces; it is the literal limb. 'of' signals letters taken from inside 'peaceful nation'.
explanation.definitionFit: This bone runs along the forearm on the little-finger side, giving the limb its rigidity.

clue.text: How could this big vegetarian fail to survive, having run so robust a constitution?

indicators.note: a constitution is a make-up, so these letters are made up into a new order

explanation.surface: Asks why so sturdy a beast died out when its body was so strong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'constitution' looks like the animal's health; it signals rearranging RUN SO ROBUST A.
explanation.definitionFit: A huge plant-eating sauropod dinosaur, now usually called Apatosaurus.

indicators.note: the word loses its tail, its final letter

parts.note: an aircraft is a plane

explanation.surface: A design drawing for an aircraft built without a tail section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailless' takes the final E off PLANE.
explanation.definitionFit: A blueprint is a detailed scheme or design drawing, a synonym.

clue.text: English river crustacean the French find toothsome

annotationWithheld.why: Printed (and scanned) as 'English river crustacean the French find toothsome': wordplay EXE+CRAB+LE gives the answer, but the definition 'toothsome' (tasty) is the opposite of EXECRABLE; presumably 'loathsome' was meant
annotationWithheld.clue: English river crustacean the French find toothsome

clue.text: Cheeky aroma some common puddings possess?

parts.note: afters is informal British slang for dessert
to possess is to have

explanation.surface: Some ordinary desserts give off a saucy smell.
explanation.walkthrough: Afters is homely British slang for the dessert course. 'Cheeky' refers to the cheeks the scent is splashed on.
explanation.definitionFit: A scented lotion splashed on the cheeks after a shave.

clue.text: Feels sad, upset yet is not likely to wither away

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disarranged, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone feels low and troubled, yet is not about to fade out of life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' looks like part of the mood, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that will not fade stays fresh and vivid, never wilting.

parts.note: Man is the Isle of Man, so making a Man of something is turning it into an island

explanation.surface: An instruction to toughen someone up and turn a boy into a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make a man of' sounds like toughening someone up; Man is the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea, so the verb means to make into an island.
explanation.definitionFit: To isolate something as on an island, the poetic verb meaning to put on an isle.

parts.note: to slough a skin is to shed it
evil is wrong, wickedness

explanation.surface: A nagging old woman is blamed for the misdeeds of Slough, the English town.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough looks like the English town in Berkshire; it is the verb, to cast off.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicious, bad-tempered woman, a scold.

clue.text: Catch fellow-batsman running back one run short?

indicators.note: one run short means one run is missing, so it is taken away
the word is read backwards, as the batsman runs back

parts.note: in cricket the batsman at the other end is your partner
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A cricketer catches out his partner, run out going back for a run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running back' reverses PARTNER to RENTRAP; 'one run short' removes one R.
explanation.definitionFit: To trap or ensnare someone is to catch them.

parts.note: a speech in praise of Daisy is a toast, and Browning suggests both the poet and a kitchen gadget browning bread

explanation.surface: A poem in praise of a girl named Daisy, perhaps by Robert Browning.
explanation.walkthrough: One who proposes a toast speaks in someone's praise; Browning looks like the poet Robert Browning but means making bread brown.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a person proposing a toast and an appliance for browning slices of bread.

clue.text: Current controller of horses at dressage

indicators.note: dressage puts horses through set movements, so the letters are put through a new arrangement

parts.note: the printed fodder, which should hold the letters of the answer

explanation.surface: Someone in charge of the horses at a dressage event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dressage' signals the anagram, but 'horses at' has two S and one T where the answer needs one S and two T: the setter's slip.
explanation.definitionFit: A variable resistor regulates the flow of electricity, so it controls an electric current.

parts.note: packaging here means selling package holidays, not boxing goods

explanation.surface: The business of making boxes and wrappers.
explanation.walkthrough: Packaging suggests cartons; it is the business of package holidays.
explanation.definitionFit: The holiday trade sells package deals of travel and lodging.

clue.text: Hollow warning of schoolboys to sailors

parts.note: cave, Latin for beware, was the schoolboy cry warning that a teacher was coming
RN, the Royal Navy, stands for sailors

explanation.surface: Schoolboys shout an empty warning to some sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: Cave (pronounced KAY-vee) was British public-school slang for 'look out!'.
explanation.definitionFit: A large underground chamber is a hollow in the rock.

clue.text: One who creates a scene in Whitehall, for example

definitions.text: One who creates a scene in Whitehall, for example

parts.words: One who creates a scene in Whitehall, for example
parts.note: Whitehall is a London theatre, and creating a scene there means setting up scenery

explanation.surface: A protester making a fuss in Whitehall, the street of government offices in London.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitehall suggests the London street of ministries and making a scene a fuss; the Whitehall is also a West End theatre, where scenes are shifted.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre crew member who moves scenery and props builds each scene behind the curtain.

indicators.note: a vessel going astern moves backwards, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a tub is a slang name for a slow ship

explanation.surface: Join a vessel that is reversing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going astern' reverses TUB to BUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that meet at a boundary touch end to end, as neighbouring plots adjoin.

parts.note: abatement taken all the way means reduced to nothing, zero, O
din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: Which deity presides over reducing noise?
explanation.walkthrough: Noise abatement means no din: O (nothing) plus DIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Odin is the chief of the Norse gods, ruler of Asgard.

indicators.note: a reflection shows things in mirror image, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
is shortens to 's, giving S

explanation.surface: Something that both shines and mirrors light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflective' reverses IT + S + A (with 'is' cut to 's) into ASTI.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti spumante is an Italian sparkling wine.

parts.note: Bottom is the weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream, and the flying class is birds

explanation.surface: The worst pupil in a group learning to fly.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottom looks like the lowest pupil; it is Nick Bottom, the weaver in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, so a weaver among birds.
explanation.definitionFit: This finch-like African bird weaves elaborate nests, a weaver among the feathered kind.

parts.note: to give ear is to pay attention

explanation.surface: An aristocrat is listened to at great length.
explanation.definitionFit: This British peer ranks above a viscount and below a marquess.

clue.text: Shaw's principled chap never in the wrong?

definitions.text: Shaw's principled chap never in the wrong?

parts.words: Shaw's principled chap never in the wrong?
parts.note: in Shaw's The Man of Destiny a national type is never found in the wrong because he does everything on principle

explanation.surface: A man of firm principle whom the playwright Shaw describes as never in error.
explanation.walkthrough: George Bernard Shaw wrote in The Man of Destiny that 'you will never find an Englishman in the wrong. He does everything on principle.'
explanation.definitionFit: A native of England, as Shaw's satirical line describes such a fellow.
